newsitem.title: USA: Poll shows Democrat leading in Georgia Senate race.
newsitem.headline: Poll shows Democrat leading in Georgia Senate race.

text.p: A moderate Georgia Democrat who hopes to replace retiring Sen. Sam Nunn has a commanding lead over his conservative Republican opponent, according to a poll published on Friday.

A telephone survey of 665 likely voters in the state put Democrat Max Cleland 16 percentage points ahead of Republican Guy Millner, while spotlighting female voters as a key electoral bloc in the Nov. 5 election.
With only a month to go before the general election, analysts said the survey could mean Republicans have little chance of capturing the seat.

"If those numbers are right, it would be an awfully big margin for Millner to overcome," said Emory University political science professor Merle Black. "Things could change. But if the race was going to tighten up, it should have done so over the summer."

Millner spokesman Stuart Roy questioned the accuracy of the poll, saying it was based on a sample audience that did not reflect the actual party breakdown of the voting electorate. He said the latest poll sponsored by the Millner campaign showed Cleland with only a four-point lead.
But Cleland noted parallel results from a separate independent poll last month showed him 12 points ahead.
"This poll reflects our positive response to our TV and just the fact that more and more people are making up their minds," the Democratic candidate said in an interview.
Friday's poll suggested the Democratic Party had succeeded in turning House Speaker Newt Gingrich of Georgia and his conservative legislative agenda into a campaign liability for Republicans.

The anti-Gingrich ploy appeared to be especially effective with female voters, who said they feared a continued Republican majority in Congress would make deep cuts in health-care programs for the poor and the elderly.
The poll was conducted Sept. 29 to Oct. 2 by Marketing Workshop Inc. for the Atlanta Journal-Constitution and WSB-TV, the local ABC affiliate. It had a 4 percentage point margin of error.
The same poll gave President Bill Clinton a 15-point lead over Republican challenger Bob Dole.
Among women surveyed, Cleland enjoyed a 25-point lead over Millner, a millionaire businessman whose outspoken opposition to abortion has won him the backing of conservative Christian groups.
He had a 15-point lead among white women, a key swing constituency which helped deliver Georgia for Clinton in 1992 and aided the Republican takeover of Congress two years later.
